w: What's tested The spleen and the thymus: their parts, what is in each part, and what each organ does How to tell the white blood cells apart, and what each one does B cells, the two kinds of T cells, and NK cells Innate versus adaptive immunity Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs, and where the B and T cells are in each Lymph nodes, the gut's lymphoid tissue and the tonsils Dr. Herr's Lecture 19, on Tuesday, November 17, starts the blood part of the course: first the blood cells, then the organs where immune cells grow up and go to work. These notes are from the slides; the lecture is Tuesday, and they will be checked against its recording. The cells of the blood Red cells are about 99 percent of the cells in blood and carry oxygen and carbon dioxide. Platelets are pieces of big bone marrow cells called megakaryocytes, and they start clotting. White cells come in two groups: the granulocytes, with obvious granules (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils), and the agranulocytes, without them (monocytes and lymphocytes). Most to least common: neutrophils (50 to 70 percent), lymphocytes (30 to 40), monocytes (2 to 8), eosinophils (1 to 4), basophils (under 1). Memory trick: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. Where the blood cells come from One stem cell splits into two lines. The lymphoid line makes the B and T cells. The myeloid line makes the red cells, the megakaryocytes (platelets), the granulocytes and the monocytes. In adults, all of it happens in the bone marrow. Innate and adaptive immunity Innate immunity is already there before any germ shows up, and it isn't aimed at anything in particular: skin and mucous membranes, acid, lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva, interferons, the eating cells (neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages) and NK cells. Adaptive immunity starts after the body meets a specific antigen, and it often remembers it. B cells make antibodies (the humoral arm), and T cells attack infected and cancerous cells (the cellular arm). The white cells one by one Neutrophil: a nucleus with several lobes, two kinds of granules (the first kind holds elastase and myeloperoxidase), and stored glycogen. The main eating cell in the blood and the first defense against bacteria. It stays in the blood about 10 hours. Eosinophil: a two-lobed nucleus and big granules that stain red. Its major basic protein punches holes in parasites. It goes up with parasites and allergies like hay fever, and it has IgE receptors. Basophil: the rarest, under 1 percent. A two-lobed nucleus and dark blue to purple granules full of heparin and histamine. It has IgE receptors and plays a big part in asthma. Monocyte: a big cell with a horseshoe-shaped nucleus. It stays in the blood about 3 days, then moves into tissue and becomes a macrophage. It eats bacteria and debris and has MHC II. Lymphocyte: a round nucleus with just a thin rim of pale cytoplasm. Small ones are B and T cells; large ones are NK cells. B cells, T cells and NK cells B cells wear IgM and IgD on their surface as antigen sensors. With help from helper T cells, they turn into plasma cells in the secondary lymphoid organs and pour out antibodies. T cells use a T cell receptor, and they only see antigen that another cell holds up on MHC. Helper T cells are CD4 and read MHC II on cells like macrophages; they send out signals that boost B, T and NK cells. Cytotoxic T cells are CD8 and read MHC I; they kill infected cells with perforins and help reject transplants and fight tumors. Trick: 4 times 2 is 8, 8 times 1 is 8. NK cells have no B or T markers and no antigen-specific receptor. They kill virus-infected and tumor cells. Their CD16 grabs the tail end of IgG, so they can kill a cell that antibodies have tagged. That is ADCC, and macrophages, neutrophils and eosinophils can do it too, with perforins, granzymes, TNF and enzymes. What the lymphoid organs do They find and get rid of germs, foreign material, transplanted cells and cancer cells. Primary organs (bone marrow and thymus) raise the B and T cells without any antigen around. Secondary organs (lymph nodes, the gut and throat lymphoid tissue, and the spleen) are where those cells meet antigen and get activated. Every lymphoid organ is built on a frame of reticular cells and type III collagen, except the thymus, whose frame is epithelioreticular cells. The bone marrow B cells and NK cells are born and grow up in the marrow, and B cells that attack the body's own tissue are removed there. T cell precursors start in the marrow but go to the thymus to finish. Before birth, the liver also makes B cells. The thymus It sits behind the top of the breastbone. It is biggest in babies and children, then from the early teens it shrinks and turns to fat. It has lymphatics going out but none coming in. Its T cell receptors get their variety by rearranging genes, and 95 to 99 percent of the T cells in it die. Its outer cortex is dark, packed with young T cells. Its inner medulla is lighter, with fewer, bigger T cells and Hassall's corpuscles, little onion-like balls of flat cells. The blood-thymus barrier (capillary wall and basement membrane, macrophages, epithelioreticular cells) keeps antigens away from the young T cells. T cell school: precursors come in through postcapillary venules, pass a first test in the cortex (positive selection) and a second in the medulla (negative selection, which removes cells that attack self), and leave as either CD4 or CD8 cells. Secondary organs Lymph nodes filter lymph, the gut and throat tissue guard the linings, and the spleen filters blood. Lymphatic vessels They start as dead-end tubes in connective tissue that soak up fluid, antigens and cells, run through lymph nodes, and empty into the subclavian veins through the thoracic duct. Lymph nodes Small bean-shaped organs with a capsule. B cells sit in the outer cortex, in follicles; T cells sit in the paracortex below it. A resting follicle is just a ball of B cells; after antigen arrives it grows a germinal center, where B cells multiply, with a mantle around it. Lymph comes in through afferent vessels and leaves through an efferent one: the lymph node is the only lymphoid organ with both. Lymphocytes from the blood get in through high endothelial venules. Nodes make mostly IgG. Dendritic cells show antigen to T cells. Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen for B cells in germinal centers but can't present it, because they have no MHC II. Gut lymphoid tissue and the tonsils MALT is loose lymphoid tissue under the linings of the gut, airways and urinary and genital tracts. Its nodules are mostly B cells, with T cells around them, and it makes IgA that is pumped into the lumen. Peyer's patches are clumps of it in the ileum, and M cells on top of them carry antigens in from the gut. The tonsils ring the back of the mouth and nose (Waldeyer's ring): palatine, lingual, pharyngeal and tubal. They have no incoming lymphatics. A child's swollen, inflamed pharyngeal tonsil (the adenoid) is adenoiditis and can block breathing. The spleen The biggest lymphoid organ, in the upper left belly. It filters blood, not lymph, so it has no incoming lymphatics. It removes old red cells and platelets, recycles iron, holds about a third of the platelets, and makes IgM and IgG. No cortex or medulla. White pulp is lymphoid tissue around a central arteriole: T cells hug the arteriole (the PALS), B cells sit in nodules beside it, and a marginal zone of macrophages and some B cells wraps around it. Red pulp, most of the spleen, is splenic cords and sinuses. In the open circulation, blood from the sheathed capillaries spills into the cords, macrophages check it, and the cells squeeze back into the sinuses through slits between rod-shaped lining cells. The sinus wall has only hoops of basal lamina, and no muscle or pericytes. Where the B and T cells are B cells: lymph node follicles, spleen nodules, gut nodules. T cells: lymph node paracortex, the spleen's PALS, the areas around the gut nodules, and the thymus.
